To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
consumers who eat less animal products hold positive attitudes towards plant based foods, and consumers who eat more animal products hold negative attitudes.
barriers towards adopting a plant based diet were identified as negative attitudes towards the taste of the products, the satiety effect of the products and the protein content of the products.

consumers with a high intake (more than 4 times a week) of either animal based products or all animal products, have negative attitudes towards plant based food, while consumers with a low intake (less than 2 times a week) have positive attitudes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
barriers and facilitators to the adoption of a more plant based food consumption.
the attitudes of the consumers towards plant based diets.
the barriers and facilitators that consumers face towards adopting a more sustainable and healthy diet.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
consumers with a high intake in all animal products and meat have negative attitudes towards plant based food, which could serve as barriers towards adopting this diet.

the results indicate that consumers with a high intake frequency of animal products hold negative attitudes towards the health and environmental effects of plant based diets, and that these attitudes serve to be barriers for the adoption of a more plant based diets.
consumers who are already consuming a plant-based diet are more likely to have positive attitudes towards plant based food.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
consumers with a high intake in animal products are not convinced that plant based diets are healthy and sustainable.
the barriers identified in the current study are similar to the barriers identified in other studies.
consumers with a low intake and consumption of animal products hold positive attitudes towards plant based food and diets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most important barrier towards adopting a plant based diet is the perception of low protein content in plant based food, followed by taste and satiety effect.
there is a need for a more positive framing of plant based diets, and a focus on the taste and availability of plant-based food.
consumers who have already adopted a more plant based diets are motivated by the same factors as those that are not yet adopting a more plant base diet.
